messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Daniel Mercer was 42, a married ship captain who had spent most of his adult life trusting his judgment at sea, when a man-made disaster on one of his voyages changed the way he moved through the world. During a routine port approach, a blast tore through the dockside loading area near his vessel, sending a concussive bang across the water and throwing debris in every direction. In the chaos he saw men in military-style uniforms and police gear rushing toward the scene, shouting orders while objects were hurled and broken in the confusion. What should have been an ordinary stop became a moment he still described as unreal and relentless: the sound, the uniforms, and the sight of things flying through the air fused into one vivid memory that kept returning without permission. Since then, those same cues had carried a special force for him. A slammed door that sounded too much like an explosion could make his chest tighten; a police officer standing outside a terminal or a soldier in uniform could pull his attention back to that dock in an instant; seeing someone angrily throw a bottle or a tool could make him flinch before he had time to think.

Daniel had come to believe that he could not rely on other people, especially when things turned dangerous. He was certain that if he let himself think about the event in full, he would not be able to handle it, and he also felt bitter that the people responsible had faced no consequences. Those beliefs made the world feel less predictable and more hostile to him. They also sharpened the power of his triggers: because he felt on guard for betrayal and danger, a uniform at a distance or a sudden bang in daily life did not feel neutral but loaded with threat, as if the disaster could break open again at any moment. He tried to keep those thoughts away, but the more he pushed them down, the more he found himself scanning for signs that something was about to go wrong.

Over the following months, Daniel’s days narrowed around safety. He avoided unfamiliar places because he could not assess the danger there, and when he was out with his wife he always chose the seat that gave him the best view of doors, windows, and exits. He became vigilant for dangerous people in restaurants, terminals, and parking lots, studying uniforms, body language, and any sudden movement. At night he had difficulty falling asleep because he needed to stay alert, and that exhaustion fed a growing willingness to hand off important responsibilities just to keep himself feeling protected. On land, he began declining situations that would have taken him into unfamiliar neighborhoods or crowded public spaces, even when they mattered to his work. He was also spending money gambling, telling himself the rush helped him distract himself or feel something other than dread for a while; in practice, those nights of trying to outrun his mind left him more unsettled afterward, and the guilt only deepened his sense that he could not trust his own judgment or the people around him.

That conviction spread into the rest of his thinking. If he gave up a responsibility, avoided a route, or stayed home rather than face a potentially risky setting, it briefly confirmed that the world could not be safely managed and that he was on his own with it. What began as caution hardened into an expectation that danger was everywhere and that only constant vigilance kept him alive. Even minor sounds on the ship, such as a metallic crash from the galley or a cargo bin dropped on the dock, could send him back into that alert state. By the time he presented for help, Daniel was exhausted by the need to watch every room, every face, and every noise, and he was frightened that this narrowing way of living was costing him his marriage and his authority as captain. He said he had finally come because he could no longer keep pretending that staying on guard was the same as being safe, and what he feared most was either losing control in front of his crew or being caught off guard by another bang, another uniform, another moment that would make the disaster feel present all over again.
